extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, poets, literary critics, and students of history/philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for investigating subjects, composing persuasive essays, and writing poetry (metre, sonnets, editing), aimed at producing coherent, philosophically-informed literary and historical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: First mode — definition-led (deductive) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a definition and deduce conclusions successively from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode assumes the initial definition as true; any small error in the definition is multiplied through successive steps, potentially producing monstrous but formally irrefragable conclusions. Its chief use is to sharpen the wit; it is the best exercitation for developing acute reasoning. Beware: unlike mathematicians (who create and control their definitions), in non-mathematical subjects you cannot 'make' things true by definition because the matters are connected with real externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second mode — historical (fact-collection) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Find truth by collecting facts and tracing them downwards (empirical/historical approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This common mode is criticised for selection problems: where to begin and end the collection, what facts to select or neglect, and how to distinguish accidental/ diseased phenomena from essential ones. Different historians may collect different classes of facts and each may 'prove' something true without reaching the whole truth. Thus historical collection alone is inadequate for arriving at the real truth in many complex subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third mode — philosophic (idea-led) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Commence with a philosophic idea or self-realizing theory that explains phenomena and makes the facts meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry your rule (idea) ready-made to measure and interpret facts: if the idea comprehends all preserved facts, gives them causal meaning, reduces miscellaneous fragments into order, and ministers strength and knowledge for practical work, then you may claim its truth. For non-mathematical sciences, a mental initiative or intuition of the ultimate aim is necessary for philosophical investigation; theory and facts must be integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the first mode — sharpening the wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive, definition-led argument is valuable as a mental exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though unreliable for arriving at empirical truth, this mode is excellent practice to sharpen intellectual acuity and logical skill (exercitation). Use it for training the mind but not as the sole route to substantive truth about real externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-guided explanation of facts (historian's craft)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make facts speak truth you must know the idea or truth which ought to be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting up as a statesman or interpreter purely on historical knowledge is unwise; analogous to buying instruments and calling oneself a musician. You must know how to 'play'—i.e., have an idea/theory that explains why events are what they are and how they interrelate; otherwise collections of facts remain miscellaneous and unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master established metres before experimenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should write for a period in one or two well-known, strictly defined metres to internalize metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are not a 'metrist' yourself, even writing in a known and approved metre often will not produce harmonious verse; inventing new metres without understanding what metre means and requires is preposterous. Recommended exercises: practice heroic couplet, octave stanza, or octo-syllabic measures to acquire a sensation (if not conscious knowledge) of metre, analogous to students conning classical verse to learn form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of budding greatness in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Key qualities in early great poetic work: fertility, condensed thought, and sweetness of rhythm/metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Shakespeare's sonnets, Venus and Adonis, Rape of Lucrece) show 'boundless fertility and laboured condensation of thought, with perfection of sweetness in rhythm and metre.' These are essentials in the budding of a great poet; later habit and consciousness bring more ease and freedom of spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnets as a continuous poem
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of sonnets can function as one continuous poem of many stanzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a group of sonnets (e.g., Shakespeare's sequence) as forming a contiguous emotional and thematic whole—'a poem of so many stanzas of fourteen lines each'—so that continuity of passion and variation of expression are maintained across individual pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of connectives — linked strain in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: A close reasoner and good writer is known by the pertinent use of connectives that create a linked strain throughout a passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective prose adheres: each sentence should connect logically to the next (not merely 'touch without adhering' like marbles in a bag). A single conjunction in a well-crafted paragraph may be essential to meaning—altering it can spoil the sense. Cultivate precise connective choices to produce cohesion and cogency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation and recasting of magazine material
rubrics_metrics.description: Collected magazine writings need recasting and condensation to form successful volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author collects pieces into books, they should personally recast and condense the material; leaving it to literary executors often results in poor editorial outcomes. Select, compress and reorganize for coherence and lasting literary effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverence for ideal truths in intellectual life
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverence arises from mysteries and ideal truths that exceed mere conceptual comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because conceptions are matters of the understanding and therefore comprehensible, they cannot inspire true reverence. Reverence is the synthesis of love and fear and is due to ideal truths which remain mysterious to the intellect. Intellectual work that aspires to depth should aim at engaging such reverence rather than only presenting comprehensible conceptions.
